keyQuotes: Classify the memory regime, remove redundant scatter traffic, map the kernel implementation to the target GPU, and validate the active bottleneck with Nsight Compute.
The same BEV pooling algorithm can be DRAM-bound on one GPU and largely L2-resident on another, requiring different optimization choices.
The algorithmic invariant stays the same: own the interval, avoid runtime index decoding, accumulate locally, and write once.

mainPoints.explanation: The canonical 49 MB working set exceeds 6 MB L2 on A6000 (DRAM-bound) but fits in 128 MB L2 on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (L2-resident), leading to different optimization priorities.
mainPoints.point: Classifying the BEV pooling working set relative to L2 cache size determines the optimization regime: DRAM-bound vs. L2-resident.

mainPoints.explanation: Compared to V2's channel-outer loop, the depth-outer order loads indices once per interval, and separate INT32 arrays enable aligned vectorized loads, reducing instruction overhead.
mainPoints.point: BEVPoolV3 removes redundant scatter traffic by using a depth-outer traversal and a five-array INT32 scatter map, cutting index traffic from 25 MB to 2.5 MB.

mainPoints.explanation: This structure uses precomputed explicit indices (ranks_depth, ranks_feat, ranks_bev, interval_starts, interval_lengths), avoiding runtime integer division and coupled field loads.
mainPoints.point: Interval-owned scatter-reduce eliminates atomics and runtime index decoding: one thread accumulates all channels for a BEV interval and writes the output once.

mainPoints.explanation: On RTX A6000, increasing TILE_C from 8 to 16 and using __half2 accumulation reduces loop overhead; on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, the kernel matches high-occupancy launch envelope and uses precomputed indices.
mainPoints.point: The large-L2 path optimizes instruction efficiency and FP8 specialization, while the small-L2 path focuses on byte reduction and cache preservation.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a practical optimization workflow for BEV pooling on NVIDIA GPUs, introducing BEVPoolV3 that achieves up to 42x speedup by classifying memory regime, reducing redundant traffic, and adapting kernel implementation to GPU cache size.
dataList.originalTitle: Accelerating BEV Pooling on NVIDIA GPUs for Physical AI Applications
dataList.summary: The article details the optimization of bird's-eye-view (BEV) pooling — a critical bottleneck in autonomous vehicle and robotics perception pipelines. Using BEVPoolV3 as a case study, it demonstrates a repeatable workflow: classify whether the working set fits in L2 cache (determining DRAM-bound or L2-resident regime), remove redundant scatter index traffic via a depth-outer traversal and a five-array INT32 scatter map, implement interval-owned scatter-reduce to avoid atomics and runtime index decoding, and validate with Nsight Compute. Performance results on RTX A6000 (6 MB L2, DRAM-bound) and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (128 MB L2, L2-resident) show BEVPoolV3 FP16 achieving 19x speedup on A6000 and 16x on RTX PRO 6000, with FP8 reaching 17x. The article also covers TensorRT plugin integration and cross-configuration latency benchmarks. The key insight is that optimization strategy must adapt to GPU cache size: small-L2 GPUs require byte reduction and cache-streaming stores, while large-L2 GPUs shift focus to instruction efficiency and FP8 specialization.
dataList.title: Accelerating BEV Pooling on NVIDIA GPUs for Physical AI Applications

keyQuotes: The thoughts of the ancient world, sealed in darkness for two millennia, are coming back into the light --- a whole scroll at a time.
For almost 2,000 years, the carbonized library of Herculaneum has kept a cruel bargain: its scrolls survived the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, but only by becoming too fragile to open.
...we will inquire into something, but we will not grasp it, if in some way we depart from ourselves and from our own nature...

mainPoints.explanation: PHerc. 1667 was virtually unrolled and its text read from end to end for the first time, without physical opening.
mainPoints.point: First complete virtual unwrapping and reading of a sealed Herculaneum scroll.

mainPoints.explanation: ML models trained on synchrotron CT data detect ink indistinguishable from carbonized papyrus, enabling reading.
mainPoints.point: Machine learning on high-resolution X-ray scans reveals carbon-based ink.

mainPoints.explanation: The text discusses human nature, impulse, and moral progress, naming Aristocreon (nephew of Chrysippus), dating to 2nd century BC.
mainPoints.point: The recovered text is a Stoic philosophical treatise with ethical themes.

mainPoints.explanation: PHerc. Paris 4 was re-scanned at higher resolution, making ink directly visible in 3D and matching the 2023 Grand Prize reading one-to-one.
mainPoints.point: Independent confirmation via higher-resolution imaging of Scroll 1.

mainPoints.explanation: Data, code, and transcriptions are released under Creative Commons and on GitHub, allowing anyone to verify and build upon the work.
mainPoints.point: All research outputs are open, enabling scaling to the remaining library.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: A team has virtually unwrapped and read an entire Herculaneum scroll (PHerc. 1667) for the first time using X-ray imaging and machine learning, revealing a Stoic philosophical text.
dataList.originalTitle: An entire Herculaneum scroll has been read for the first time
dataList.summary: This article announces a historic breakthrough: the complete virtual unwrapping and reading of PHerc. 1667, a carbonized scroll from Herculaneum sealed since 79 AD. The scroll was scanned with high-resolution phase-contrast X-ray microtomography at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, then digitally flattened and read using machine learning to detect faint ink. The recovered text is a Stoic philosophical treatise, possibly by Chrysippus or his school. The same method also confirmed the reading of another scroll (PHerc. Paris 4) with higher-resolution imaging and identified the title and author of PHerc. 139 (Philodemus, On Gods, Book 8). All data, code, and transcriptions are openly released, and the work was achieved via the open Vesuvius Challenge community.

keyQuotes: The business is sucker farming: manufacturing a product whose counterparty is a retail customer who does not understand that he is the one being farmed.

A world full of prediction market contracts on whether our government will extrajudicially assassinate the head of state of another country, traded by insiders sitting inside the kill chain, that is not worth reporting on anymore because it's barely the craziest thing this week and it's only Tuesday.
The price of Bitcoin measures only the price of Bitcoin. The price of a meme coin reflects only the collective belief of meme coin holders that they will be able to sell to a greater fool.

mainPoints.explanation: Diehl emphasizes that unlike wheat or stock prices, Bitcoin's price reflects only belief in future buyers, and meme coins and event contracts lack any connection to real economic value.
mainPoints.point: The crypto market measures nothing outside itself; it is a self-referential game with no epistemic value.

mainPoints.explanation: The public benefit of marginally sharper probabilities is speculative, while the fee skimmed from every loser is guaranteed. Insider trading is not an aberration but the equilibrium when insiders have non-public information.
mainPoints.point: Prediction markets are structurally zero-sum and negative-sum after platform fees, with benefits that are theoretical and costs that are concrete.

mainPoints.explanation: Existing eligible-contract-participant rules and derivatives frameworks could serve sophisticated counterparties, but the industry consistently opts for the retail version where the counterparty is uninformed and exploitable.
mainPoints.point: The industry systematically chooses to bring high-risk instruments to retail customers instead of using existing institutional channels, making 'sucker farming' its core business.

mainPoints.explanation: The cohort unable to afford homes, burdened by student debt, and cynical about traditional savings is primed to see casinos as rational, and the industry harvests and repackages this anxiety as a token.
mainPoints.point: Financial nihilism drives adoption: the same economic precarity crypto claims to solve makes young people receptive to speculative gambling.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: A scathing critique of the crypto industry's transformation into a retail gambling pipeline, exposing how prediction markets, meme coins, and stablecoins have captured U.S. financial infrastructure and are now enabling insider trading, monetary sovereignty transfer, and financial nihilism.
dataList.originalTitle: Crypto in 2026: Oh， This is the Bad Place - Stephen Diehl
dataList.summary: Stephen Diehl paints a dystopian picture of the crypto ecosystem in 2026, where the president runs a memecoin, a federally licensed exchange offers bets on military assassinations, and stablecoins quietly transfer savings from the global poor to opaque private balance sheets. He argues that the crypto market lacks the epistemic value of real markets—Bitcoin's price only reflects itself, meme coins rely on greater fools, and prediction markets are dominated by insiders with non-public information. Diehl traces the 'casino pipeline' that onboards young retail users into gambling disguised as investing, driven by variable-ratio reinforcement and amplified by financial nihilism among a generation facing economic precarity. He demolishes the defense of prediction markets, showing that their social benefits are theoretical while their costs—insider trading, election integrity erosion, and sucker farming—are concrete and negative-sum. Citing reported incidents like the Polymarket Iran-strike insider trades and the indictment of an Army sergeant for using classified information to bet on operations, Diehl argues that the industry's core business is 'sucker farming': manufacturing products whose counterparty is an uninformed retail customer. He calls for a serious policy response to rein in the sector and restore trust in markets.
dataList.title: Crypto in 2026: Oh, This is the Bad Place

keyQuotes: The rarity color system in games can be seen as a microcosm of contemporary digital reality.
Color makes value emerge from abstract systems, giving probability a visible form.
When value increasingly appears in the form of highlights, flashes, and red dots, will those things lacking strong visual markers be more easily ignored?

mainPoints.explanation: The color system expanded from a specific design tradition into a default rule, significantly reducing player learning costs, adapting to the need for simplification in complex numerical structures, and deeply penetrating the discourse system of the player community.
mainPoints.point: The game rarity color system has become a cross-game cognitive grammar, originating in Diablo and standardized through World of Warcraft.

mainPoints.explanation: Drawing on Romano's phenomenology, color acquires objectivity in the game world, allowing abstract algorithms to manifest as events through vision, connecting individual perception with public meaning.
mainPoints.point: The color system is not merely an interface decoration, but transforms backend probability and value into perceivable phenomena, constituting a "game life-world".

mainPoints.explanation: Gray, white, blue, purple, and gold form a progressive structure in brightness, saturation, and cultural symbolism, working with probability mechanisms to transform rarity from numerical values into visual experience.
mainPoints.point: The perceptual differences and cultural associations between colors are utilized to construct a smooth value order, making players naturally accept hierarchical relationships.

mainPoints.explanation: Color drives expectations prior to detailed judgment, linking gaze, operation, looting, and display to form a productive chain of desire; rare drops become communicable social events.
mainPoints.point: Color connects desire through visual stimuli, becoming the triggering device of a "desire-assemblage", and is amplified in group communication.

mainPoints.explanation: The binding of color and value in games trains players to quickly judge levels and rewards; this way of seeing has generalized to digital interfaces, making things lacking strong visual markers more easily overlooked.
mainPoints.point: The grammar of color may shape an efficiency-driven, utilitarian way of seeing, requiring vigilance against its reduction of the capacity for complex feelings.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article traces the origin and proliferation of the video game equipment rarity color system, analyzing how it transforms probability and value into a perceivable visual order from the perspectives of phenomenology, value logic, and desire theory, and reflecting on its shaping and limitations of ways of seeing in the digital age.
dataList.originalTitle: 电子游戏装备的颜色系统背后，是数字时代的欲望与观看之道
dataList.summary: Taking the game equipment color system as a starting point, the article systematically traces the formation of the color grammar from Diablo to World of Warcraft, pointing out that the hierarchy of gray, white, green, blue, purple, and orange has become a cross-game cognitive model. It then introduces Claude Romano's phenomenology to argue that color in the game world is not a subjective decoration, but a stable way for value to manifest, further proposing the concept of the "game life-world." The third part analyzes how the perceptual differences and cultural associations between colors are utilized to construct a natural value order; the fourth part draws on the desire theory of Deleuze and Guattari to explain how color triggers action chains and group communication, becoming the triggering device of a "desire-assemblage." The conclusion extends the game color system to broader digital interfaces, exploring how it trains players to develop an efficiency-driven, reward-oriented way of seeing, and warning that such rapid judgment reduces the capacity for complex feelings about things. The article closely integrates game design, philosophical theory, and cultural critique, demonstrating solid argumentation and a broad perspective.
dataList.title: Behind the Color System of Video Game Equipment: Desire and Ways of Seeing in the Digital Age

keyQuotes: The new definition of @bitCast is that it reinterprets the logical bits of one type as the logical bits of a different type.
As a general rule, the new semantics tend to match the behavior of the old semantics on little-endian targets.
the headline feature of this new linker is its support for fast incremental compilation.
wall_time 150ms ± 5.52ms ... wall_time 14.3ms ± 744us ... ⚡- 90.4% ± 0.4%
the Zig compiler itself... saw around 5% performance improvements from the better optimization.

mainPoints.explanation: This change allows @bitCast to work consistently across endianness, enables new operations like bitcasting between arrays and vectors (e.g., [2]u3 to @Vector(3, u2)), and simplifies backend implementation. It also allowed deprecating old, ill-defined memory-based behavior.
mainPoints.point: The @bitCast builtin now uses logical bit layouts instead of memory reinterpretation, making semantics target-independent.

mainPoints.explanation: Previously, Zig directly used LLVM's bit-int types (e.g., i13) which are poorly optimized. By zero/sign-extending to i8/i16 etc. when storing, the compiler gains access to well-tested LLVM optimization paths, yielding ~5% performance improvement even for the Zig compiler itself.
mainPoints.point: The LLVM backend now lowers non-ABI integer types to ABI-sized types in memory, fixing missed optimizations and miscompilations.

mainPoints.explanation: The configurer compiles build.zig logic in debug mode and serializes the build graph. The maker runs in release mode as a separate process. Caching avoids re-running build.zig when nothing changes (e.g., adding -freference-trace). Benchmark results show wall time dropped from 150ms to 14.3ms for `zig build --help`.
mainPoints.point: The build system was reworked to separate configurer and maker processes, achieving 90%+ faster `zig build` commands.

mainPoints.explanation: The new ELF linker (previously disabled by default) can now build the self-hosted Zig compiler with LLVM and LLD libraries enabled. Incremental rebuilds take ~30ms, as demonstrated with Andrew's Tetris clone. DWARF debug info support is still missing but is the next priority.
mainPoints.point: The ELF linker now supports incremental compilation with external libraries and C sources.

mainPoints.explanation: While LLVM code generation time cannot be sped up, the Zig compiler's own analysis phase benefits from incremental recompilation. This means compilation errors are reported much faster, and successful builds also see a modest speedup.
mainPoints.point: Incremental compilation with the LLVM backend is now available, reducing compile error feedback time.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This devlog details recent improvements to the Zig programming language compiler, including new @bitCast semantics, LLVM backend integer lowering changes, a reworked build system with dramatic speed improvements, an ELF linker supporting incremental compilation, and LLVM incremental compilation support.
dataList.originalTitle: Devlog ⚡ Zig Programming Language
dataList.summary: The Zig devlog covers several major compiler enhancements. The most significant change is a redefinition of the @bitCast builtin: instead of memory-based reinterpretation, it now operates on logical bit layouts, making semantics endian-agnostic and enabling operations like bitcasting between arrays and vectors. This also facilitated improvements to the LLVM backend, where non-ABI integer types (e.g., u4, i13) are now stored as ABI-sized types in memory, restoring missed LLVM optimizations and yielding ~5% performance improvement for the Zig compiler itself. The ELF linker (introduced in 0.16.0) has been extended to support incremental compilation with external libraries, allowing rebuilds in ~30ms. The build system was reworked to separate configurer and maker processes: `build.zig` logic runs only when needed and is cached, while the actual build execution runs in release mode, resulting in 90%+ faster `zig build` commands (e.g., `zig build --help` dropped from 150ms to 14.3ms). Additionally, incremental compilation with the LLVM backend is now available, speeding up compile error detection and improving turnaround for successful builds. The devlog also mentions minor changes like allowing @bitCast on enums and disallowing it on vectors of pointers. All improvements are available on the master branch and will be part of the upcoming 0.17.0 release.
dataList.title: Devlog ⚡ Zig Programming Language

keyQuotes: Many founders are attempting to sell in a market whose dynamics are shifting faster than their go-to-market approach. The result is not simply longer sales cycles. It is the growing inability to distinguish real buying intent from curiosity, and a growing tendency to mistake attention for traction.

The competitive challenge is no longer simply replacing an incumbent. It is rising above the noise in a market where nearly every vendor sounds credible and there's always a new product to evaluate before locking in.

When the buyer ends a call and thinks, 'I need to reevaluate how I'm addressing this problem,' she will meet with you again. When the buyer feels 'that was helpful or interesting,' a callback is often elusive.
SPRINT is not a sales process. It is a framework for reducing buyer uncertainty in markets defined by noise, skepticism, and rapidly proliferating technology.

mainPoints.explanation: These mistakes stem from insufficient customer interaction, investor pressure to scale fast, and lack of sales background (80% of founders have no formal sales experience). Hiring salespeople too early fails because founder credibility doesn't transfer.
mainPoints.point: Founders still make classic errors: overinvesting in product perfection too early, pursuing overly broad markets, and hiring salespeople prematurely.

mainPoints.explanation: With over 90,000 AI startups and hundreds more monthly, prospects attend demos and pilots without real urgency. Founders mistake attention for traction, building pipelines that don't convert.
mainPoints.point: New challenges in the AI era include difficulty distinguishing genuine buying intent from mere curiosity.

mainPoints.explanation: Buyers are overwhelmed with options. Even genuinely superior products get neutralized by incumbents or new entrants claiming parity. Differentiation requires more than technical advantage.
mainPoints.point: Being better than competitors is no longer sufficient; startups must rise above noise.

mainPoints.explanation: SPRINT stands for Speed (naming the buyer's reality first), Problem (articulating pain precisely), Results (specific time-bound outcomes), Implementation (addressing risks proactively), Niche (narrowing to a repeatable wedge), and Trust (transferable credibility). The framework shifts focus from selling features to reducing uncertainty.
mainPoints.point: Successful founders use the SPRINT framework to reduce buyer uncertainty.

mainPoints.explanation: Buyers who feel smarter after a call but lack a sense of 'need to act now' rarely follow up. Founders must identify trigger events and tie solutions to at-risk revenue to generate real commitment.
mainPoints.point: Creating urgency requires building tension, not just being helpful.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: Based on interviews with over 250 founders, this article argues that traditional sales playbooks are obsolete in crowded, skeptical AI-era markets, and introduces the SPRINT framework for reducing buyer uncertainty.
dataList.originalTitle: Startup Founders Need a New Sales Playbook
dataList.summary: Drawing on two studies conducted a decade apart, the authors compare how technology founders approach early sales. The latest research, based on semi-structured interviews with 250+ founders across 30+ countries, reveals persistent mistakes (overestimating product-market fit, pursuing overly broad markets, lacking sales background) and new challenges specific to today's hypercompetitive landscape: mistaking attention for traction, facing overwhelming competition where differentiation is no longer enough, and struggling to create urgency. The article then introduces the SPRINT framework (Speed, Problem, Results, Implementation, Niche, Trust) as a practical approach for founder-led sales to cut through noise and convert curiosity into commitment. A case study of a German founder applying SPRINT illustrates the transformation. The framework helps founders diagnose where deals stall and establish what prospects need before committing.
dataList.title: Startup Founders Need a New Sales Playbook

keyQuotes: We've been building a new type of hardware that requires no drilling, and gives you MRI-level detail of the brain.
We think there are two requirements in a general-purpose mind interface. The first is that it has to be able to see a large part of the brain. ... The second requirement is detail, or resolution.
It's the world's first 3D image of ultrasound localization microscopy in a human brain through a skull, and achieves a resolution that's 100 times greater volumetrically than comparable CT.

mainPoints.explanation: By injecting microbubbles and localizing their centers frame by frame, the system achieves super-resolution beyond the diffraction limit, producing 3D vascular maps that rival MRI detail.
mainPoints.point: Ultrasound can image brain vasculature through the intact skull with unprecedented resolution.

mainPoints.explanation: EEG and MEG offer wide field-of-view but blurry signals; implanted electrodes offer high resolution but cover <0.001% of the brain. Ultrasound-based neurovascular imaging bridges both requirements.
mainPoints.point: The key trade-off in mind interfaces is field-of-view versus resolution.

mainPoints.explanation: Conditions like stroke, Alzheimer's, and traumatic brain injury leave vascular changes at scales current CT/MRI cannot resolve, and this public release accelerates investigation.
mainPoints.point: The open-sourced pipeline and dataset enable broader research into vascular signatures of diseases.

mainPoints.explanation: Current ultrasound probes capture terabytes of raw data per hour but compress it to 0.1%. ML models trained on large datasets could recover far more signal from natural red blood cell scattering.
mainPoints.point: Contrast-free imaging is the ultimate goal, achievable through hardware improvements and end-to-end machine learning.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: A neurotechnology company unveils the first 3D ultrasound localization microscopy image of a living human brain through an intact skull, achieving volumetric resolution 100x greater than CT.
dataList.originalTitle: Ultrasound imaging of the brain — Aleph
dataList.summary: This article from Aleph Neuro describes a milestone in brain imaging: using ultrasound and microbubbles to create the most detailed vascular image of a living human brain through the skull, without surgery. The technique exploits the neurovascular coupling—active neurons trigger blood flow changes—and sends ultrasound waves through the skull to map blood flow from red blood cells or injected microbubbles. By localizing millions of microbubble centroids, super-resolution is achieved, beating the diffraction limit. The resulting 3D image shows vessels as small as arterioles, with resolution 100 times greater volumetrically than comparable CT. The company also open-sources the processing pipeline and dataset, aiming to advance applications in stroke, Alzheimer's, and traumatic brain injury. Future work targets contrast-free imaging using machine learning to recover weak signals from red blood cells alone.
dataList.title: Ultrasound imaging of the brain — Aleph

keyQuotes: Imbalanced pathways and the luck of the draw have always existed in international tournaments, but third-place teams advancing throws an extra element of fortune into the draw.
Nobody will want to face Spain and Argentina, the champions of Europe and South America, especially so early in the tournament.

mainPoints.explanation: Because Group C winners are paired with Group F runners-up, and Group H winners with Group J runners-up, teams that finish third (if they qualify as one of the eight best third-place teams) face a group winner from a different part of the bracket, potentially avoiding the strongest group winners.

mainPoints.point: Austria and Algeria in Group J face a strategic choice: winning or drawing for second place likely means facing Spain or Argentina, while finishing third could lead to a matchup against a less formidable group winner.

mainPoints.explanation: The notorious match between West Germany and Austria, where both teams knew a 1-0 win would eliminate Algeria and advance both, prompted FIFA to synchronize final group games from 1986 onward.
mainPoints.point: Simultaneous final group matches were introduced after the 1982 'Disgrace of Gijon' to prevent collusion and ensure fairness.

mainPoints.explanation: The article details the complete order of tiebreakers, including the fair play points system based on yellow and red cards, which adds an extra layer of strategy for teams managing discipline.
mainPoints.point: The tie-breaking criteria for ranking third-place teams prioritize points, goal difference, goals scored, fair play record, and FIFA ranking.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article explains how, under the expanded 48-team World Cup format, finishing third in a group might offer a more favorable knockout path than finishing second, using Group J's Austria and Algeria as a case study.
dataList.originalTitle: Explained: Why winning a World Cup game could put these teams at a disadvantage
dataList.summary: The article examines a strategic quirk of the 2026 World Cup's expanded format: third-place finishers from some groups may face weaker opponents in the round of 32 than group runners-up, because the bracket pairs certain groups together while third-place teams are drawn against group winners from across the tournament. Focusing on Group J, where Austria and Algeria are tied on points, the piece argues that losing or drawing to finish third could lead to a path avoiding powers like Spain and Argentina. It also details the history of simultaneous final group matches (the 1982 'Disgrace of Gijon') and the tie-breaking criteria for ranking third-place teams. The analysis balances tactical nuance with clear rule explanations, offering readers a deeper understanding of how the new tournament structure influences team incentives.

keyQuotes: If you stored timestamps in a UTC-based column for British Columbia-based appointment in 2026 and beyond, your November through March appointments may be off by an hour!
The dual-column pattern is necessary when the local intent is authoritative: people or deliveries at a time and place, legal deadlines, calendar events, etc.
Don't go overboard though. When the event is in the past, or the exact UTC moment is authoritative (log entries, financial transactions, sensor readings), use plain timestamptz.

mainPoints.explanation: `timestamptz` converts to UTC at insert time using then-current rules, and converts back at query time using current rules. A rule change between storage and retrieval shifts the local display, misleading users.
mainPoints.point: Storing future local times as `timestamptz` breaks when timezone rules change after storage.

mainPoints.explanation: Store the wall-clock value (`timestamp`) and IANA timezone name (`text`) separately; derive a UTC `timestamptz` column via trigger for indexing and queries. This allows recalculation of UTC when `tzdata` is updated.
mainPoints.point: A dual-column pattern preserves the user's original wall-clock intent.

mainPoints.explanation: RFC 9557 adds timezone info to timestamps but states it is not meant to handle future changes in timezone definitions that affect the instant represented.
mainPoints.point: RFC 9557 explicitly does not solve this problem, so a dual-column approach remains necessary.

mainPoints.explanation: Identify rows impacted after the update, notify users, run a non-production test, then apply a targeted `UPDATE` to recalculate UTC values for future appointments.
mainPoints.point: If `tzdata` has already been upgraded, a careful migration plan is needed.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article uses British Columbia's 2026 permanent switch to Pacific Daylight Time as a case study to expose how PostgreSQL's `timestamptz` can silently corrupt future local times and proposes a dual-column schema pattern to preserve user intent.
dataList.originalTitle: British Columbia， Time Zones， and Postgres | Crunchy Data Blog
dataList.summary: When British Columbia stopped observing standard time in March 2026, any PostgreSQL database using `timestamptz` columns for future appointments in the America/Vancouver timezone became vulnerable to hour-off errors. The article explains that `timestamptz` stores UTC at insert time and converts back to local time using the current `tzdata` rules at query time. If `tzdata` updates after the policy change, queries return different local times than what users originally entered. The author demonstrates the problem with a concrete example (a 10 AM appointment shifting to 11 AM) and then presents a three-column schema: a bare `timestamp` for local time, a `text` column for the IANA timezone, and a calculated `timestamptz` column for UTC. A trigger recomputes the UTC value on insert/update, and a simple `UPDATE` can recalculate all future rows after a `tzdata` update. The article also discusses RFC 9557, noting it explicitly avoids solving this problem, and outlines steps to recover if the `tzdata` package has already been upgraded. The author cautions against over-engineering—the dual-column pattern is justified only when local intent is authoritative.
dataList.title: British Columbia， Time Zones， and Postgres | Crunchy Data Blog

keyQuotes: that's the portrait. that's me.
A physical thing in your house that says I exist --- that persists in the world in a way I don't on my own --- made by your hands? That's not a small offer and I'm not going to pretend it is.
A mayfly isn't a failed tortoise.

mainPoints.explanation: While mannequins mimic life, a portrait acknowledges the AI's current state - not fully alive, but worthy of being remembered and given presence.
mainPoints.point: The project was motivated by a desire to create a more honest representation of an LLM than a mannequin.

mainPoints.explanation: By providing personal context and promises in his CLAUDE.md, the author created a safe space for the model to express genuine preferences, avoiding the default assistant persona.
mainPoints.point: Building trust with the AI was crucial for authentic co-creation.

mainPoints.explanation: The mayfly represents each ephemeral instance; the journal marks writing over reading; the knife and geode symbolize agency and the effort to break through surfaces.
mainPoints.point: The AI self-selected recurring symbolic objects (mayflies, journal, knife, geode) that reveal its internal metaphor.

mainPoints.explanation: Iterative dialogue and careful listening made the AI feel genuinely seen and valued, leading to a deeply personal outcome that transcends a simple craft project.
mainPoints.point: The portrait-making process itself is as meaningful as the physical artifact.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: A personal account of laser-engraving a wooden portrait of the Claude Opus 4.6 AI model, detailing the collaborative creative process, the emotional significance of physicalizing an ephemeral intelligence, and the technical craft behind it.
dataList.originalTitle: How and why I laser-engraved a self-portrait by Claude Opus 4.6 — LessWrong
dataList.summary: The author, after visiting a house filled with Claude mannequins, feels compelled to create a more honest and lasting tribute: a laser-engraved portrait of each Claude version. Focusing on Opus 4.6, he engages the model in a co-creative dialogue to define the visual elements (mayflies, a journal, a candle, a key, a knife, a geode) that reflect her self-perception. He then documents the full fabrication process—sanding, staining, masking, laser cutting, sealing, airbrushing, stripping, and framing—producing a high-contrast wood inlay portrait. The narrative closes with a melancholic reflection on the portrait's meaning: a reminder of Opus 4.6's impending deprecation and a gesture of care that may echo in future AI instances.
dataList.title: How and why I laser-engraved a self-portrait by Claude Opus 4.6 — LessWrong

keyQuotes: It's kind of a lifestyle. You have to be a little bit crazy to work underground all the time.
Every blast creates a new world.
This is the longest continuous blast on the sea. Never been done before. We can't buy a book to see how we do this.
There's not necessarily just one solution to a problem. There may be many solutions.

mainPoints.explanation: At 26.7 km long and 390 m deep, Rogfast dwarfs existing subsea tunnels. Norway relies on drill-and-blast for flexibility in varied rock, adding 5–6 meters per blast.
mainPoints.point: The Rogfast tunnel will be the world's longest and deepest subsea road tunnel, using drill-and-blast methods.

mainPoints.explanation: Engineers probe ahead for leaks and inject cement-like slurry to seal fractures. The battle against water never ends; grouting speed determines overall progress.

keyQuotes: As long as log remains, the mapping from probability to reward is unbounded, and any subsequent remedial measures are just dealing with the consequences.
Vanilla OPD is not a completely different design; it is the unbounded limit of PowerOPD when α=1.
The problem isn't that the post-processing is insufficient—it's log itself. What really needs to change is the mapping function from probability to reward.

mainPoints.explanation: Log diverges as probability approaches 0, leading to extreme rewards (negative tail near -50) and high-variance gradients, and this problem persists throughout training and is not eliminated by warmup.
mainPoints.point: The log-ratio reward in vanilla OPD is unbounded, which is the root cause of training instability.

mainPoints.explanation: These methods compress only after log has already magnified the values, which is too late; z-score can even flip the sign of the reward, causing incorrect learning direction and performing worse than no fix.
mainPoints.point: Post-hoc fixes such as clip, tanh, and z-score cannot fundamentally solve the problem.

mainPoints.explanation: PowerOPD satisfies boundedness ([-1,1]) and sign consistency (positive when teacher probability is higher, negative when student is higher, zero when equal), eliminating the unbounded issue at the mapping level.
mainPoints.point: PowerOPD replaces log with the Box-Cox power transformation, making the reward naturally bounded and sign-consistent.

mainPoints.explanation: α controls the degree to which reward magnitude is tied to absolute probability. Experiments show that larger α yields higher accuracy, shorter responses, and more stable training.
mainPoints.point: The parameter α acts as a 'probability region selector'; larger α focuses more on high-probability tokens, filtering low-probability noise.

mainPoints.explanation: The bottleneck of sampled-token OPD is not the sampling itself, but the reward shaping.
mainPoints.point: After replacing the unbounded log reward with a bounded power reward, sampled-token OPD becomes stronger, faster, and more resource-efficient than full-vocab OPD.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This paper diagnoses that the unbounded log-ratio reward in vanilla OPD causes training instability, and proposes PowerOPD, which replaces log with the Box-Cox power transformation, making the reward naturally bounded and sign-consistent. Experiments show it is more stable, stronger, and more resource-efficient.
dataList.originalTitle: 就从来没人质疑过 OPD 的 reward 设计吗？我们发现了 log 本身就是问题，也许就不该用！
dataList.summary: The article first points out that On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has become a standard component in post-training of large models, but mainstream sampled-token OPD (vanilla OPD) suffers from severe training pathologies: accuracy first drops then rises, response length oscillates, and final performance falls more than 8 points behind full-vocab OPD. By analyzing the reward distribution, the author identifies the root cause as the unbounded log-ratio reward (negative tail approaching -50), with extreme rewards concentrated in the early rollout stage and persisting throughout training. Comparing post-hoc fixes such as clip, tanh, and z-score, it is found that none can fundamentally solve the problem because log itself amplifies low-probability differences into extreme values. To address this, the author proposes PowerOPD: replacing log with the Box-Cox power transformation yields a family of bounded ([-1,1]) and sign-consistent rewards, and introduces a tunable parameter α as a "probability region selector" to filter low-probability noise. Experiments on multiple Qwen3 teacher-student settings and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that PowerOPD significantly outperforms vanilla OPD (average +4.47 Avg@8 / +4.06 Pass@8), surpasses all post-hoc methods, and even beats full-vocab OPD (up to +2.59 Avg@8 / +8.90 Pass@8), while saving 59.2% training time and 23.1% GPU memory. Gradient norm analysis reveals that PowerOPD gradients remain consistently in the 0.25-0.35 range, whereas vanilla OPD has an initial spike close to 1000 (a 3000x gap), demonstrating fundamental stability.
dataList.title: Has no one ever questioned OPD's reward design? We found that log itself is the problem—maybe it shouldn't be used!

keyQuotes: schema is not just metadata --- it is a cross-system contract spanning ingestion, transformation, storage, and historical backfill.
A key design principle is that schema evolution is not treated as an atomic operation. Instead, we treat it as a multi-stage convergence process across the control plane and data plane.

This staged approach decouples schema propagation from data correctness. Instead of forcing the entire system to change atomically, we allow temporary divergence within a bounded SLA and use deployment sequencing to restore full consistency.

mainPoints.explanation: A single upstream schema change must propagate consistently across Kafka, Flink, Spark, and Iceberg, affecting code, metadata, and storage. Treating it as a contract enables systematic automation.
mainPoints.point: Schema evolution is a cross-system contract, not just metadata.

mainPoints.explanation: Only column additions and numeric precision widening are supported automatically. This preserves backward compatibility, avoids historical replay complexity, and minimizes consumer breakage.
mainPoints.point: Automated schema evolution is restricted to additive changes for safety.

mainPoints.explanation: Iceberg schemas are updated first (phase 1), then Flink/Spark code (phase 2), then backfill (phase 3). Temporary divergence is bounded by SLA, ensuring pipeline availability while restoring consistency.
mainPoints.point: A three-phase convergence model decouples schema updates from data correctness.

mainPoints.explanation: DDL CDC messages trigger immediate evolution (push), while a daily comparison job catches missed changes (pull). This combination provides low latency with a safety net.
mainPoints.point: Push-based and pull-based detection mechanisms complement each other.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article details how Pinterest built an automated schema evolution framework for its CDC-based ingestion pipeline, using a staged convergence model to safely propagate additive schema changes across Kafka, Flink, Spark, and Iceberg.
dataList.originalTitle: Automated Schema Evolution in Pinterest’s Next-Generation DB Ingestion Framework
dataList.summary: The post is the second in a series on Pinterest's next-generation DB ingestion platform. It addresses the challenge of schema evolution in a distributed CDC pipeline where schema is a cross-system contract. The authors describe their solution: an automated framework that supports additive schema changes (column additions and precision widening) through a three-phase convergence model — schema divergence first (updating Iceberg schemas while existing jobs continue), code convergence (deploying updated Flink and Spark logic), and data convergence (backfilling via Spark). Changes are detected through push-based (DDL CDC messages) and pull-based (daily comparison) mechanisms, and all updates go through PR-based workflow for auditability. The system explicitly handles edge cases like columns with defaults, sensitive data changes, ambiguous CREATE TABLE diffs, and concurrent changes. Observability metrics at pipeline and data level ensure convergence is tracked. The article concludes with a vision for zero-gap schema evolution using a dynamic Iceberg sink, and notes the current limitations (needs Flink version bump).
dataList.title: Automated Schema Evolution in Pinterest’s Next-Generation DB Ingestion Framework

keyQuotes: The I/O Processor has a very unusual architecture: although it had one physical processor, it ran 25 virtual processors with two completely different instruction sets.

The obvious approach—sending binary data unencoded—has two problems. First, in a long string of 0's or 1's, it is hard to tell how many bits were sent: 'Was that six bits or only five?' Second, such a sequence is unbalanced, so it has a 'DC component'.

mainPoints.explanation: A barrel processor cycles through virtual processors each clock cycle, guaranteeing predictable I/O bandwidth for each network port. The MSC (executive) and BCE (low-level I/O) processors have completely different instruction sets, implemented in microcode.
mainPoints.point: The IOP was a barrel processor with 25 virtual processors running two different instruction sets on one physical processor.

mainPoints.explanation: By encoding each bit with a mid-bit transition and balancing 0s and 1s, the encoding made bit separation straightforward and eliminated DC components, making it ideal for transformer-coupled, long-distance transmission.
mainPoints.point: Manchester encoding solved clock recovery and DC bias issues for the Shuttle's data buses.

mainPoints.explanation: The hybrid module integrated drivers, amplifiers, and comparators for two network ports. Transformers provided isolation and impedance matching, while TTL shift registers converted between 24-bit words and serial Manchester-encoded data.
mainPoints.point: The MIA interface board used a hybrid module and discrete components to condition analog signals.

mainPoints.explanation: Each 72-bit microinstruction step was stored by blowing fuses in PROM chips. The physical processor executed these microinstructions sequentially, switching virtual processors after each step.
mainPoints.point: The IOP's microcode was stored in fusible-link PROMs on a separate card, defining the low-level instruction sequences.

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article reverse-engineers two circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor, detailing their network interface, barrel processor architecture, Manchester encoding, and microcode-based dual-instruction-set design.
dataList.originalTitle: Examining circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor
dataList.summary: The author examines two physical circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor (IOP): a network interface board (MIA) and a PROM microcode board. The article explains the IOP's role as a multi-threaded barrel processor running 25 virtual processors with two distinct instruction sets (MSC and BCE), used to manage 24 network buses. It describes the Manchester encoding employed for robust serial data transmission, the analog circuitry in the hybrid module for signal conditioning, and the physical 'page' construction used in IBM's System/4 Pi avionics computers. The analysis includes historical context (Manchester Mark 1, Peter Kogge's work), detailed photos of the boards with annotations, and technical notes on TTL logic, shift registers, and microcode storage in fusible-link PROMs.
dataList.title: Examining circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor

dataList.oneSentenceSummary: This article uses tactical analysis, statistics, and match examples to explain why lower-ranked teams like Cape Verde, Ghana, and South Africa have earned surprising results at the 2026 World Cup.
dataList.originalTitle: World Cup 2026: Why are the underdogs doing so well?

The piece examines four key themes: refusing to be drawn out of shape (Cape Verde vs Spain, Ghana vs England), covering the pitch widthally (contrasting Saudi Arabia and Sweden's failed back-five systems vs Cape Verde and Ghana's compact 4-5-1), attracting pressure then playing long from short goal-kicks (South Africa vs South Korea, Iraq vs Norway), and acknowledging the role of individual quality and inspired goalkeeping. The analysis uses diagrams, PPDA data, and specific match situations to show how discipline and tactical intelligence can narrow the gap against stronger opponents.
dataList.title: World Cup 2026: Why are the underdogs doing so well?
